title: EF Core — change tracking, N+1, migrations, EF Core 10
exp: EF Core questions at 4 YOE are almost never "how do you add a migration." They're "explain how change tracking works" and "what is the N+1 problem." These connect directly to your production work.
pts: **Change tracking:** EF monitors all queried entities by default, comparing snapshots on `SaveChanges()`. Only modified properties generate SQL
**`AsNoTracking()`:** disables change tracking — typically 20–40% faster for read-only queries
**N+1 problem:** load N entities, access navigation property in a loop → 1+N database round-trips. Fix: `.Include(o => o.Customer)`
**EF Core 10 — named query filters:** multiple `HasQueryFilter()` per entity type, selectively disable individual filters
**EF Core 10 — native JSON columns:** model JSON columns directly without manual serialization — great for metadata in a compliance platform
`DbContext` is already a Unit of Work — `SaveChanges()` flushes all changes in one transaction

qa.q: What is the N+1 problem in EF Core and how do you fix it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** N+1 happens when you load N entities and then access a navigation property on each in a loop — triggering 1 additional query per entity (total: 1 + N queries). Fix with .Include(e => e.RelatedEntity) to eagerly load in a single JOIN query. Detect it by enabling EF Core query logging — you'll see the same query repeated N times.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** SQL Server query processor constructs a logical tree, estimates cardinality using statistics, and selects physical operators (Nested Loops, Hash Join, or Merge Join) based on cost and sorted indexes.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Cartesian products or missing join predicates can cause exponential disk tempdb spilling, memory grant exhaustion, and query timeouts under concurrent load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Nested loops excel for indexed small lookups; Hash joins handle large unsorted sets at the cost of higher tempdb and memory grant usage.

**Elevator Pitch:** For read-only queries where you won't call SaveChanges() on the retrieved entities — API responses, reports, exports. EF Core skips creating change-tracking snapshots, reducing memory usage and processing time by typically 20–40%. Never use it if you need to update those entities afterward.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Garbage Collector uses generational collection (Gen 0, 1, 2, LOH, POH) with mark-sweep-compact phases. Span<T> provides stack-allocated contiguous representation.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Excessive allocations of large objects (>85KB) trigger frequent Gen 2 / LOH collections, causing GC pause spikes and high CPU.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Span<T> and Memory<T> eliminate heap allocations and copy costs, but ref structs cannot be boxed or captured in async state machines.

qa.q: How does EF Core's DbContext relate to the Repository and Unit of Work patterns?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** DbContext already implements both. It's a Unit of Work because SaveChanges() flushes all pending changes in a single transaction. It's a Repository because DbSet<T> provides query, add, update, and delete operations. Adding an extra Repository wrapper usually just adds indirection without benefit — unless you need to support multiple ORMs or deep unit-test isolation.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transaction log (WAL) guarantees ACID. Isolation levels control locking (Shared/Exclusive) vs versioning (RCSI/Snapshot) in tempdb.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Long-running transactions hold locks, causing cascading blocking chains, deadlocks, and transaction log bloat.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** RCSI eliminates reader-writer blocking but increases tempdb I/O and row-version overhead.
